title: The Mexican martyrs (21 May)
hookLine: Christopher Magallanes and companions killed during the Cristero years

lines: A CRY, A PRAYER, LAST WORDS.
cards: ¡Viva Cristo Rey! Long live Christ the King. In Mexico, in the years of the Cristero conflict, those words could be a battle cry, a password, a prayer, or the last thing someone said.
In those years, in that country, calling Christ king could cost you your life. Today, the Mexican martyrs.

teach.b: Some background, kept simple. There was a time when Mexico's government passed harsh laws limiting the Church: priests registered and restricted, schools and orders closed.
In protest, the bishops suspended public Masses across the country. Some Catholics took up arms, and the fighters came to be called Cristeros.
It was a real war, with violence on more than one side, and the Church doesn't canonize a war.
What the Church honors on this day is different: Christopher Magallanes, a parish priest, and a group of companions, priests among them, who were killed for their faith during those years.

teach.h: A PRIEST WHO DIDN'T TAKE UP ARMS.
teach.b: Tradition remembers Father Magallanes as a pastor who ran a seminary in secret, cared for his people, and did not urge them to take up arms.
When he was arrested and brought to be shot, the story goes, he gave away what he had, said he was innocent, and forgave those who were about to kill him.
Some of the martyrs, tradition says, died with that cry on their lips: Viva Cristo Rey. Here's the line under the whole day.

Jesus, in the Douay-Rheims: "Love your enemies: do good to them that hate you: and pray for them that persecute and calumniate you." That's the strange part of these martyrs. Their cry sounds like a battle shout.
But the ones the Church remembers here are honored for dying without hatred.
Long live Christ the King, said by a man forgiving the soldiers in front of him: a king, in this faith, crowned with thorns.

how: On 21 May the Church keeps an optional memorial of Saint Christopher Magallanes and companions; in Mexico, Catholics often pray for their country and visit shrines connected to the martyrs.

a Cristero general who led Catholic fighters

games.q: the Mexican martyrs — tap the pairs.

s: the Church canonized the Cristero war
it honors martyrs killed for their faith, not the war itself.
Father Magallanes, the story goes, forgave his killers
tradition remembers him forgiving those about to shoot him.
Viva Cristo Rey was only ever a battle cry
it was also a prayer, and for some martyrs, last words.

games.q: you're a parish priest in Mexico. public Masses have stopped, and some of your people want to take up arms. what do you do?
o: keep serving your people in secret.
games.why: tradition remembers Magallanes running a seminary in secret and caring for his people. he was killed anyway, forgiving his executioners.

practice: Bring Mexico to mind as it is today: its cities and villages, its families and parishes, people living with violence and people working for peace, those who have gone north and those waiting at home.
If you pray, ask the Mexican martyrs to pray for Mexico, or say their cry quietly, long live Christ the King; if you don't, hold its people in mind with goodwill, one face at a time.

wordCard.voice: Christopher Magallanes, the priest remembered with his companions as the Mexican martyrs, killed in the Cristero years, honored for dying without hatred.

orig.note: Spanish: long live Christ the King — the cry of the Mexican martyrs.

carryVoice: Your line: long live Christ the King. Said without hatred, the cry becomes a prayer. That's day nine hundred ninety-four.
